Private Mopar Collection Hides 1968 Hemi GTX Ragtop 1-of-1, Owner Turned Down a Superbird for It
15 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Some people just win the lottery. Others develops sophisticated schemes and systems designed to improve the odds and up the chances at a get-rich-fast’n’easy jackpot, some just walk in, pick a random ticket, and become millionaires. That’s about the same statistical randomness that made an Oregon Moparhead strike the deal of a lifetime several times in a row. This time, it’s a Hemi GTX ragtop.
Rarely does a collector car combine one-of-a-kind factory provenance with a lighting-strikes-thrice mechanical reunion across 3,000 miles of United States of Automobile. Well, prepare for yet another unbelievable story from the Mopar history treasure trove of Gary Myers' workshop in Vernonia, Oregon.
The man is probably the coolest Mopar collector anywhere, and not necessarily for his cars (although he does own a special gathering of holy grails), but also for the stories that come with each and every one of those. I’m telling you right here, in writing, the man is a great candidate for case studies on how does luck work. Of course, someone would have to quantify luck in the restrained, limited confinements of science before such a venture would be practicable, but we digress.
Troy Bergeron, the larger-than-life gearhead and Moparhead from Mopars5150 YouTube channel came face-to-face with a 1968 Plymouth Hemi GTX convertible finished in deep GG1 Forest Green metallic over a white interior, white top, and white stripes. And that’s just the beginning of the options list. In fact, it’s far easier to say what didn’t come on it, because it’s just one add-on – the black-out hood treatment. Everything else was put on it.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 You must be wondering who’d buy a Hemi Mopar loaded with everything, and for what. To show off is the answer to the “why,” but this car wasn’t ordered by a private client with a knack for high-horse cheap B-body ChryCo automobiles. I know, the GTX was the top dog in the Plymouth lineup of intermediates during its tenure (1967-1971), but it was still a product of the lowest-cost division in the Chrysler Motors Corporation hierarchy.
Plymouth introduced the GTX as a special trim on the Belvedere in 1967 as the "Gentleman's Muscle Car," pairing upscale interior appointments and distinctive styling with standard big-block power. If that sounds even remotely familiar, let me remind you of the road runner. No, not the Road Runner from 1968, but the one from 1967. The one Dodge introduced. Yes, Dodge. You know, the Coronet R/T? The Fratzog boys dubbed it “the road runner.”
Plymouth countered with the GTX package on its run-of-the-mill mid-sizer, the trusty Belvedere. Produced as a standalone model from 1968 through 1971—before transitioning into an optional performance package on the Road Runner between 1972 and 1974—the GTX received Chrysler's sleekly contoured second-generation B-body architecture for the 1968 model year, resulting in 18,940 total units built.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The model year was the all-time highwater mark for the moniker, which had the misfortune of being in the same division, at the same time, in the same place with the lowest-buck, highest-bang Mopar of them all – the Plymouth Road Runner.
Of those 18,940 examples assembled for 1968, 17,914 were two-door hardtops and only 1,026 were two-door convertibles. While the vast majority carried the standard 375-hp (380-PS) 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Super Commando V8, a mere 446 buyers checked the box for the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 rated at 425 hp (431 PS) and 490 lb-ft (664 Nm) of torque. Only 36 of those 1968 Hemi GTXs were convertibles.
Within that microscopic run of 36 Hemi drop-tops built for the United States market, just 24 were equipped with the heavy-duty A727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission, while 12 received the 4-speed manual. According to Mopar historian Galen Govier, who personally inspected and decoded Gary's convertible, only a dozen examples were previously known to exist in the registry, alongside two additional survivors Gary knows of in Canada, bringing the surviving total to 14.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Even among those 14 remaining relics, Gary's car stands alone as a documented 1-of-1 configuration. Built as Chrysler's West Coast Public Relations vehicle for 1968, it is one of the two green 1968 Hemi GTX convertibles ever produced, and the only one paired with a white interior. Because PR fleet cars were loaded to showcase the catalog, it carries every single factory option except the hood blackout paint. I assume it wouldn’t have made much of a visual impact to put black next to dark green?
That exhaustive option sheet even includes a bizarre factory three-passenger rear seatbelt option across a convertible rear bench that measures barely 4 feet (1.2 meters) wide. Of course, safety wasn’t the end-of-worlds topic that has grown into today, but it was still nice to show prospects that the division cared for the occasional back seat occupants.
To ensure the cabin remained period-perfect, Gary spent $1,000 for a mint original woodgrain steering wheel pulled from a vintage driving simulator and paid $440 at the Mopars at the Strip show in Las Vegas for an uncracked original green center console.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 When Gary first acquired the convertible—having walked away from a $7,000 deal on a disassembled Sublime 1970 Superbird in central Oregon so he could afford the GTX—the car lacked its original engine and transmission. Some would say that’s unlucky, but Gary is not accustomed to that notion. Not by a long mile.
He tracked down a properly-coded 1968 Hemi block out of a Dodge Coronet, and then spotted an East Coast magazine advertisement from an elderly transmission builder selling a genuine 1968 Hemi TorqueFlite unit for $1,200.
The seller explained that a drag racer had brought a brand-new 1968 Hemi B-body into his shop back in 1968 to swap in a manual-valve-body race transmission, leaving the factory automatic untouched under the shop workbench for over more than three decades. After making Gary promise to tear it apart and inspect the internals before running it, the seller accepted a $400 deposit and had a friend crate the transmission for air freight.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Shipped across the continent to Portland via Forward Air, the transmission arrived at Gary's shop, where a glance at the stamped serial pad nearly knocked him off his feet. The vehicle identification number stamped into the transmission case was one single digit ahead of his GTX's VIN.
Against astronomical odds, an East Coast transmission sitting under a bench since 1968 had come from the Hemi car built immediately ahead of his West Coast convertible PR showboater. Care to debate luck now?
When Gary opened the transmission pump as promised, the factory BorgWarner ink stamps were still freshly visible across the clutch packs. That’s how new the original, numbers-matching car was – most probably, the one who ditched it didn’t even drive his car.
Delighted by the miracle and amused that the seller's crate builder had warned the old man about how Gary would scam him, our Oregon Moparhead mailed a final check with an extra $100 enclosed, instructing the seller to take his skeptical friend out to lunch and tell him that was how West Coast car guys kept their word. Pay it forward? Attracting abundance? I prefer “righteous man,” and everything good in Gary’s life is definitely well deserved.
